Delicious 1972 Airstream Argosy Is the Cutest Retro Home Tiny Home You'll See This Week
16 photos
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings
The retro look won't work for everyone, but that's ok: we're all different, and as such, we're probably destined not to like the same things. That said, even someone who is passionately against the sugary retro style will probably appreciate the appeal of this Airstream Argosy turned into a tiny home.
The original rounded series of Argosy travel trailers was in production for about 8 years, between 1972 and 1980, but the exact number of produced units remains a mystery. They're now Airstream unicorns, but back in the day, Airstream regarded them more like the poor and simple cousin from out of town that you're ashamed to be seen in public with.
Brochures referred to them as "the almost Airstream" or the entry-level Airstream: a travel trailer that looked like an Airstream and was supposedly built with the same attention to quality work and quality materials as an Airstream, but that was not , in fact, an Airstream .
An Argosy was cheaper because it was usually built with discarded materials from the main Airstream factory. It was assembled at another facility and did not get you into the Airstream clubs and owners community, though dealers would still service it.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings An Argosy was painted, which the "real" Airstream, with its iconic silver bullet sheen of polished, riveted aluminum, never was. An Argosy was, in short, the lesser Airstream: an Airstream by birth but not one by education and, as such, never quite welcome at the Airstream family table.
Times have changed.
With them, so has the RV community attitude to the Argosy, the painted aluminum, to the point where today they're icons that become coveted collectibles . They change hands for high prices as well, as you'd expect from a collectible, even if they're no longer able to travel the country as they were once meant to do.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings This is the case with the unit we're looking at today, a 1972 Argosy turned into a tiny house. Any Airstream, whether Argosy or not, was imagined as a sort of tiny house on wheels, if only on account of the fact that it comes with all the creature comforts and space for the entire family.
This one still has wheels but most likely won't be using them. It's being sold out of South Carolina as a fixed guest house slash rental slash permanent home for a couple, with a completely redone interior and accessories that are optional but necessary. It's still an Argosy, and a gorgeous one at it, but it's also different.
The biggest change to the original layout of the 22-footer (6.7 meters) is the removal of the onboard bathroom to create a larger footprint and more moving space. Instead, the current owner added a separate bathhouse with a spacious shower, a nice vanity with storage, and what looks like a plumbed toilet.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings With the bathhouse, the listing also mentions the possibility of getting the deck at an extra price. It would make sense for the future owner to choose the bundle, since they're all styled to match.
The Argosy, described as one of the first to roll off the production line (not that this is truly relevant), retains the two-tone paintjob the old models had – this one in striking turquoise and white. Inside, you get all-plywood walls and ceiling, with refurbished floors and wood-trimmed windows.
You also get colorful furniture in shades that match whatever retro expectations you set when you first saw the exterior. Turquoise cabinets, bright yellow sleeping areas, white and turquoise tiled counters, and bright green trimming to add an even more striking pop of color. It's all very retro but also sweet, delicious, and cozy.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings The listing mentions a queen bed in the rear bedroom space, with a smart TV mounted on a wall and a large storage compartment underneath. A large arch to the entrance of the bedroom creates some sense of separation, though not actual privacy for whoever is sleeping inside.
At the other end of the trailer, in what functions as the living room, is a sofa in bright yellow. It's a sleeper sofa, so you can probably accommodate one or two overnight guests in case of an emergency, assuming they don't mind the absence of an indoor bathroom and the aforementioned lack of privacy.
The middle portion of the trailer is split between the galley kitchen and the dining space, both finished in matching tiles with cute flower patterns. You have a two-burner induction cooktop, a large sink with a telescopic faucet, and a small under-the-counter retro fridge in the kitchen, with space to dine or get some work done across the way.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings Also included but not shown with photos with the listing is a microwave, pots and pans compatible with the induction cooktop, a new AC unit, updated plumbing, and upgraded hardware.
Storage in the kitchen space is limited to cabinets under the counter, with some extra spaces to be filled on the opposite side. Opting to not have overhead cabinets helps to remove visual clutter – a smart choice, considering the bright colors at play here. There is such a thing as too much of a good thing.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings This Argosy tiny home "combines classic vintage character with thoughtful updates and fun, colorful personality," the listing says . You can get this neat combination of neat things for an asking price of $59,999, which doesn't include the bathhouse or the matching deck.
Or you can take it all in visually, like a delicious treat - and trip down memory lane.
